solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Injury from kick aimed at player after three from Messi

parts.note: Messi is Argentinian, and 'three' in Spanish is tres
a pass is a kick aimed at a teammate

explanation.surface: A footballer hurt by a kick meant for a teammate, just after Messi scored a hat-trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three from Messi' is the language Messi speaks, not a count of his goals. In law, a trespass is any wrongful act that injures someone, not only stepping on land.
explanation.definitionFit: In old legal and biblical usage a trespass is a wrong or injury done to another.

clue.text: For puzzling last word, missing first letter

indicators.note: puzzling means confusing, so the letters are mixed up
missing first letter means the opening letter of the word last is dropped

parts.note: the fodder, before its first letter goes

explanation.surface: A puzzled request for the final word, which is missing its first letter.
explanation.walkthrough: LAST without its first letter is AST; ASTWORD is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Towards can mean for, as in money towards the cost, meaning going to help pay it.

clue.text: Time can be found reversing

parts.note: things that can be found ARE, in the sense of exist

explanation.surface: A claim that time can be found by going backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter stretches 'can be found' to mean 'exist', as in 'there are wolves here': the plural verb ARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: an era is a span of history, one way of measuring time.

clue.text: Oval filled at lunchtime, maybe pair batted incredibly

indicators.note: an incredible result is one scrambled beyond belief

explanation.surface: A cricket report: at the Oval ground at lunch, the batting pair had done amazingly well.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground, and the whole clue is cricket until you see 'Oval' as a shape: a pitta is an oval flatbread split and filled for lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitta is an oval flatbread often filled with salad or meat as a lunchtime sandwich; 'maybe' marks it as one example.

clue.text: Fat root spliced in case of subsidence

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of subsidence
to get spliced is slang for to marry

explanation.surface: A thick tree root joined into the wall of a building to hold it up where the ground has sunk.
explanation.walkthrough: A swede is a large yellow-fleshed turnip, known as a rutabaga in North America.
explanation.definitionFit: A swede is a large swollen root vegetable.

clue.text: Large section of church died apostate

parts.note: L = large, as on clothing labels
the apse is the rounded end of a church
d. = died, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A big part of the church died out after abandoning its faith.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last word, an adjective: a lapsed Catholic is one who has left the faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapsed describes someone who no longer practises their religion, as an apostate does.

clue.text: Connect with answer yet?

parts.note: A = answer, as in Q and A
yet = but, as in 'small yet strong'

explanation.surface: An impatient question: has the answer clicked yet?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Connect with' reads like joining up with a person; here it is one plot of land touching another.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that abut meet and join at an edge.

clue.text: Setting up funds, visit Washington, a friend having cased it

parts.note: to see a doctor is to visit one

explanation.surface: Advice for raising money: go to Washington and bring a friend who has checked the place out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cased' is the thieves' sense of scouting a place before a job, here it simply means holding inside, as a case holds its contents.
explanation.definitionFit: Seed capital is the money used to set up a new business.

clue.text: Very scratched from stumble across dancer in club

indicators.note: V is struck out of the longer word, as a runner is scratched from a race

parts.note: to stumble across something is to discover it

explanation.surface: A clubber got badly grazed after tripping over a dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: A discoer, one who goes to discos, is a rare word; it falls out of DISCOVER once V is gone.
explanation.definitionFit: A discoer is someone who dances at discos, the dance clubs.

clue.text: A bit of woodwork irritated lawyers

parts.note: the Bar is the body of barristers

explanation.surface: Some carpentry annoyed the lawyers.
explanation.walkthrough: In football commentary 'the woodwork' means the goal frame, even though it is now metal; the crossbar is its top.
explanation.definitionFit: The crossbar is the horizontal part of the goal, one bit of what commentators call the woodwork.

clue.text: With alien agitators on planet, show who's boss

explanation.surface: With alien troublemakers landing on Earth, it is time to show them who is in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The planet is a word to be written in, not the scene of an invasion.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear the trousers is to be the one in charge, traditionally in a household.

clue.text: Cautious states led by king during revolt

indicators.note: during means within, so the king and states go inside the revolt

parts.note: a rise, as in a rising, is a revolt

indicators.note: led by means the king's letter goes in front

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A report that a king took the lead in states during an uprising.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone risk-averse avoids danger, a hyphenated synonym of cautious.

clue.text: Small point about retaining unpopular player performing badly for City

parts.note: on = about, as in 'a talk on birds'
a ham is an actor who overacts

explanation.surface: A little dig at a disliked footballer who played poorly for City.
explanation.walkthrough: The football surface makes 'player' a footballer; it is an actor. Southampton is a port city on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Southampton is one of England's cities, a port on the south coast.

clue.text: Feature of cathedral music, probably also of the choir

indicators.note: says the answer is also part of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Something typical of music in a cathedral, and of its choir too.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is long and ends on 'probably': a cathedral's vast space usually makes sound echo.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathedrals are so cavernous that music sung in them usually echoes.

clue.text: Be useful too, nag ordered girl

indicators.note: ordered means put in a new order, so those letters are rearranged

parts.note: a miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A girl tells a horse to make itself useful as well.
explanation.walkthrough: TOONAG 'ordered' gives NOTGOA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that would not go amiss would be welcome, an idiom for being useful.

clue.text: Team not finishing wine by itself

definitions.note: 'by itself' is short for 'multiplied by itself'

indicators.note: 'not finishing' cuts a letter off

explanation.surface: A team drinks wine on its own and does not finish it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By itself' reads as 'alone'; it is the arithmetic sense, a number multiplied by itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Maths sense: a squared number is one multiplied by itself, and the clue drops the word 'multiplied'.

clue.text: Mud on ground covering island, time to get off

indicators.note: covering means wrapping round, so the island's letters go inside
ground means crushed or milled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Muck spread over an island, and then it is time to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get off' is the definition, with 'to' kept so it reads as a verb; 'ground' here is milled, not land.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismount is to get off a horse or bicycle.

clue.text: Comic error putting half human on British throne

indicators.note: putting one thing on another sets their order, here the half-word after the rest
in an across answer on means placed after

parts.note: the throne is slang for the toilet, the loo

indicators.note: half means only half the word is kept

explanation.surface: A slapstick gaffe: half a person perched on a British toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of PERSON is PER. 'Throne' is slang for the toilet, and 'loo' is British for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A blooper is an embarrassing mistake, especially one in a broadcast that people laugh at.

clue.text: Judges again pardon separating parents

parts.note: to rear children is to parent them
'Eh?' and 'Pardon?' both ask someone to repeat themselves

explanation.surface: A court reconsiders its pardon, splitting up a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parents' is the verb (raises children), not mother and father; 'pardon' is the word you say when you have not heard.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal sense: a court hearing a case a second time is judging it again.

clue.text: Archangel's censure upset Jacob's wife

parts.note: Leah, Jacob's first wife in Genesis

explanation.surface: An archangel's rebuke upsets Jacob's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob married two sisters, Leah and Rachel; only Leah fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael is one of the archangels named in scripture.

clue.text: Twisted tootsie sounded OK

indicators.note: sounded means spoken aloud, so the answer is what the words sound like

parts.note: wry means twisted and a tootsie is a toe

explanation.surface: A twisted toe sounded fine after all.
explanation.walkthrough: WRY TOE said aloud sounds like RIGHT-OH; tootsie is a childish word for a toe.
explanation.definitionFit: Right-oh is a dated British expression of agreement, much like okay.

clue.text: Unlucky fellow rid of cold? Not so

indicators.note: rid of means losing, so the cold letter goes

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: An unlucky man has shaken off his cold, or has he?
explanation.definitionFit: Hapless means having no luck, ill-fated.

clue.text: Use machine to raise papa out of bed, taking minutes

parts.note: Papa is P in the phonetic alphabet
up = out of bed; its U comes first

explanation.surface: Using a machine to haul Dad out of bed, slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise' belongs with the definition: to pump water is to raise it by machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the verb sense: water pumped from a well is raised by machine.

clue.text: Batter on fish is rubbish

explanation.surface: A verdict on a fish-and-chip shop: the batter is awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' is the fish-shop coating in the surface but the verb 'hit' in the wordplay. Codswallop is British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang synonym: talk that is nonsense can be called either word.

clue.text: Only five parts to decode

parts.note: V is five in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Just five pieces of a puzzle to crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' reads as pieces; it is a verb, V parting SOLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: cracking a code or a crossword clue means working it out.

clue.text: Gentle hits reflected fight that's not serious

indicators.note: a reflection shows the word back to front

explanation.surface: A few soft blows show the fight was never serious.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nearly defines the answer twice: light taps are what a trivial spat involves.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a brief, petty quarrel is a squabble rather than a real fight.

clue.text: Tea MP arranged with lieutenant with two more to come

indicators.note: the letters are put in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An MP's tea party organised alongside an army officer, with two more guests due.
explanation.walkthrough: Antepenultimate means third from last, so two more follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: The antepenultimate item is third from the end, with two more still to come.

clue.text: Middle section of walk is circular part

indicators.note: take the central letters of MARCH

parts.note: to walk is to MARCH; drop its first and last letters

explanation.surface: The central stretch of a walk forms a loop.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of 'walk' itself is AL, which leads nowhere: first turn walk into MARCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometry sense: a curved piece cut from a circle's edge is what the word names.

clue.text: Biologist's woolly article boring near the end

indicators.note: a drill boring into wood goes inside it

parts.note: late = near the end, as in late in the day

explanation.surface: A biologist's fleecy jumper, a dull thing near the end of its life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' is not dull here but drilling: AN bores into LATE. Lanate is a technical word, hence 'Biologist's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lanate is the biological term for woolly, covered in woolly hairs.

clue.text: Hose between the sheets in Spooner's aforementioned crate

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: aforementioned = said; its S sound swaps with the B of BOX
a crate is a box; with an S in front it becomes SOX, spelt SOCKS

explanation.surface: Stockings hidden in the bed inside a crate, as Spooner might describe it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hose' is stockings or socks, not a garden hosepipe; 'between the sheets' is simply in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedsocks are socks worn in bed, so hosiery between the sheets.
